title: Gambling: An Addiction Your Brain Can't Pull The Plug On
subtitle: A conversation with Dr. Daniel Kaufmann, Director of Gaming Services at Kindbridge Behavioral Health
body_html:
My readers know: I work a lot. My work at Radial is as a co-founcer of a Brain Medicine company. We provide healthcare to patients. There is a domain in which most therapists aren’t the most expert—it’s gambling and process addiction. I’m friends with a team called Kindbridge. I met Kindbridge in the WhatIf Ventures accelerator a lifetime ago!

The good news? Help for gambling and process addiction is available. AND additional training for therapists and health professionals is also available …now!

That is right—CEUs, which allow one to get all the way to certification, are available from the Kindbridge Institute.

l had a sit down and chat with the director of Kindbridge’s research and education efforts to talk about gambling and process addiction, how it can be understood, the scale of the problem we're talking about, and what people can do for help.

Owen Muir: Welcome to the Frontier Psychiatrists!

Daniel Kaufmann: My name is Dr. Daniel Kaufmann. I have a PhD in Counselor Education and Supervision, and I am licensed in several states as a professional counselor or licensed mental health counselor. I’m a qualified supervisor, and I’m an internationally certified gambling counselor and gaming disorder certificate holder.

Owen: Amazing. And in this context, you join us from a corporate gig.

Daniel: Yes, I am the Director of Gaming Services at Kindbridge Behavioral Health. I provide supervision and certification guidance for all clinicians and coaching staff, and I am the Director of the Kindbridge Learning Center, our online CEU learning management system.

Owen: I met the team at Kindbridge many years ago when we went through the What If Ventures Accelerator together. I was working with a different company at the time. I’m a psychiatrist, as you’ve probably heard. I’ve heard a little bit of the story of gaming and gambling disorder and other process addictions, but the audience might not be familiar. Can you tell us a little bit about the problem you’re dealing with at KindBridge, and how you're helping people in your role as a doctor of teaching to deal with it?

Daniel: One of the most important roles that I serve is that I became, last year, an editor for the American Society of Addiction Medicine for their upcoming textbook on process and behavioral addictions. I just got to speak on the main stage at their annual conference last week. We were talking about AI integrations in healthcare, which is a slightly different topic, and then in a breakout session, I was talking about gambling, video games, sex, and pornography, and integrating those topics into the already well-existing healthcare setting for psychiatry and mental health services.

Owen: I thought gambling and pornography and addiction... this all “just sounds like fun!” Is it a problem?

Daniel: Absolutely. They are all extremely fun. They activate the same reward centers that drugs and chemical substances activate, that sex activates, that eating your favorite foods activates, that exercising, that buying a thing you’ve been looking to shop for for a very long time.

The human mind is driven to find these moments, to get that dopamine reward, and to feel good about what we’ve just achieved. And for a small percentage of people, there is no limit or boundary to what they will move, ignore, or overlook in order to prioritize seeking that chemical release.

For those people, they tend to get hooked on activities that are easily repeatable and have low barriers to dopamine access. Now, actual success is a different story, but dopamine success, they can experience these even in the course of failure, because it’s triggered by anticipation rather than result.

Owen: Oh, my! So, if I’m hearing you correctly, there’s a brain chemistry we call dopamine. Is that in a specific part of the brain or circuit in the brain?

Daniel: Well, as a licensed mental health counselor, not necessarily a PhD in neuroscience, I always like to make sure I stay within my scope.

Owen: I can do this bit if it helps.

Daniel: Yeah. I know that the various processes that trigger dopamine and serotonin flow from the ventral tegmental area into the frontal lobe, activating executive functioning and bad decision-making, and putting you in situations where you’re going to face consequences. But in the moment, it feels worth it, because the thing you’re doing, it’s so easy to feel the chemical that you’re craving. Then, in the aftermath, a lot of times there is a realization of, what have I done? But it’s not a strong enough realization to change the behavior without some very targeted decisions, without seeking out self-help, without going through a 12-step process, or a treatment protocol, or going to residential treatment and detoxifying yourself from the access to that behavior or activity.

Owen: I am a physician, so I get to talk a little more freely about brain circuits, because I actually work actively with modulating these circuits in my work. We have an area called the nucleus accumbens, where the dopamine neurons project. So when you say dopaminergic release, it’s releasing on neurons with dopamine receptors in the nucleus accumbens, the reward center of the brain.

What I heard from you is that there are some people who essentially have more sensitive reward centers that are just going to go, go, go when they have the anticipation of the reward, not even the reward itself.

Daniel: In gambling, that is huge, and in video gaming, it can also be huge. In sex, orgasm is typically the thing you’re seeking, so that’s less anticipatory and more result-oriented, but you still get the buildup and the different activities that you’re watching or consuming or participating in.

It is largely about the anticipation, the planning process. Sometimes the thrill comes from the deceit and tricking other people. Or even in gambling, the process of doing a money management structure that you get hooked on. Like, I’m gonna transfer money from this on Monday, I’m gonna move it on Tuesday, I’m gonna gamble the whole afternoon away, or the next 20 minutes on Wednesday, depending on how big my bets are. The results will cut me off, because you gamble to extinction, essentially.

Owen: No one’s ever said, “I’ve got so much extra cocaine.”

Daniel: That’s true. I want to just bring up that, in some ways, as bizarre as this is going to sound, as a mental health counselor, we run into people with substance-based addictions, too. You will pass out or overdose and need medical attention when you push your body to that limit. You do risk, sometimes, the loss of life.

In gambling, you don’t necessarily do that, meaning you can push the problem even farther, the consequences even deeper. Because your body doesn’t have that limit where you pass out, and you’re not taking this drug for the next 8 hours, buddy.

Owen: Because you literally can’t incapacitate yourself from gambling. You can drink too much, and your brain will just go, consciousness off. And you can’t keep drinking when you’re unconscious.

Daniel: There is no person I’ve ever heard who thinks that if I just drink one more time, I will never have to drink again, I will be cured. With gambling, specifically, the fantasy of having all this money out of nowhere just from one very lucky moment will create a gambler’s fallacy, or a sunk cost bias, where I can’t give up, because I’ve already put so much money into this activity, the slot machine, or betting on your favorite sports league, and we’re so close to the moment where the pot is worth so much. If I quit now, I know I’m not going to win, and I owe it to myself to put myself in position to have the chance to win. So you can’t quit now, because then you’ll feel like a loser.

Owen: If you quit now, then you can’t win. And I’m so close!

Daniel: So close. Exactly.

The Scope of the Problem

Owen: We’re talking about it so people understand what it is. Tell me a little bit about the scope of the problem. How big of a problem is this right now? Maybe we’ll start just in the U.S. Who is it the biggest problem for? Who’s most vulnerable? Who’s doing it? Has it changed in the past couple years, or has it always been like this?

Daniel: One of the most well-funded explorations of the question for gambling occurred in 1999, where the U.S. government brought in some of the best researchers to do a really sound study, really strong sample, and it generated this insight that 1 to 3 percent of people in the general population at some point in their life will gamble in a way that meets criteria for gambling disorder. At the time, it would have been an impulse control disorder, and then 14 years after that, the DSM-5 moved it into the non-substance-based addiction category.

In 2013, to coincide with that, there were several places that attempted a replication study. The problem is, you screen different ways. Some people just use the DSM criteria, which is 9 criteria and a yes-no setup. The NORC diagnostic screen really is just using the DSM and 9 questions. Other people will use the South Oaks Gambling Screen, which is over 20 questions, gets a little bit more deep information, has a different threshold for saying “at risk” and confirming a diagnosis. So you can read some studies, they’ll say 5 to 7 percent. I tend to just say either 2 to 4 or 1 to 3 percent of the general population. But once you start gambling frequently, you’re not part of the general population. I think that’s the important thing for people to understand. That lineup of 100 people, randomly picking out 2 or 3 that meet gambling disorder criteria, that’s the general population, with regular people, including a percentage of people that don’t have any predisposition for any addiction issues.

Owen: That is somewhere between as common as schizophrenia and 3 to 4 times as common as schizophrenia. And everyone would agree that schizophrenia is a real problem. And my impression is that the barriers to gambling have dropped precipitously. Is that factual?

Daniel: Yeah, so this is where the big problem is with 1999 and 2013 being the best sources of data. Back in 2017 and 2018, we opened the floodgates for what kind of gambling is legal.

Owen: Hold on, I just gotta check my parlay. Oh, no. Wait. I got distracted by the fact that I have a device on me all the time that we didn’t have in 2013, and certainly not in 1999. What’s happening now? Let’s bring us up to speed.

Daniel: Now you have sports betting. Gambling is completely legal when you watch any professional or collegiate sport. All of the advertising is either for gambling or alcohol, and then in April and March, you get ads for doing your taxes, but then more alcohol and more gambling.

I actually, just as a personal note here, have stopped watching professional sports events entirely. Because it’s too much.

Owen: It’s like being at work?

Daniel: It is, to some extent. It just isn’t worth my time to watch it, because advertising is clearly the product, the game is secondary now. That’s how I feel watching it. The goal is not; the Lakers and the Rockets are playing this week. 20 years ago, you would watch, and you would actually care who’s going to win. But now you have fantasy sports, you just want the player that’s on your team to score more than 25 or get more than 10 assists, and so that’s like a secondary fantasy of what you’re watching. You couldn't care less about the Lakers or the Rockets.

On the topic of not caring about the teams or the players, you’re really just looking at, "Am I gonna win money for myself? What I want to know is who’s gonna win the series, who’s gonna win the championship?” And I don’t care about them trying to convince me to download an app and create my own league that doesn’t actually exist. I feel like I don’t fit in with the people watching sports anymore.

Owen: So they’ve ruined sports for you?

Daniel: For me, yes, but for many people, they’ve made it more appealing. And a lot of these people may not even realize they have a gambling problem, except for the very small text at the bottom of the screen during these ads that say, “gambling problem, call 1-800-WHATEVER.” By the way, the national helpline number changed, which is going to cause all sorts of confusion as well. Because of who owns that number, and some internal strife between the New Jersey Council and the NCPG. You’re going to have a slew of people who are calling the wrong number now. And you know who has their stuff together? The people asking you to gamble. So it’s really important for the people who are offering resources and recovery options to have their stuff together in these days as well.

How Devastating Is It?

Owen: How devastating is gambling as a problem?

Daniel: It’s much more devastating than the last time we collected national data to understand it, because there’s so many different avenues to participate in gambling all day. You don’t have to go to a casino anymore. Every smart device that we have in our pockets has more appealing, engagement-driven, manipulative apps on it than what you would find in a casino.

Owen: You could just be trying to sell me on a problem. Compare the devastation from gambling disorder to something else we would accept as bad. How bad is gambling disorder in terms of something comparable? A disability scale, another health condition, heart attack, something.

Daniel: I may be a biased sample for this, because my entire career, except for maybe the first 4 years of being a mental health counselor, were specifically focused on gambling.

Owen: How bad is it for your patients?

Daniel: It is a bad enough problem that I can have a full private practice in 2013, just saying on Psychology Today that I treat gambling, being in Central Florida. With gambling, you have the mental health side, and you have the crippling, often six-figure, maybe seven-figure financial hole that they’ve created for themselves.

Owen: And there are plenty of people who are willing to get you hooked on debt. Their entire industry is based on getting vulnerable people to take out more loans than they can practically afford.

Daniel: I’ve never tried to do this myself, because I don’t gamble, but from what I’ve heard from my clients, you can get more dollars approved for a personal loan in a casino than if you apply on Credit Karma or anywhere else. They want you to owe that money. Your wins did not even belong to you.

Owen: What’s the suicide rate, by the way? Because I focus a lot on this newsletter on suicide. How bad is that?

Daniel: It is comparable to disorders like bipolar disorder, and the only real psychiatric condition that has a higher suicide rate than gambling is schizophrenia.

Owen: So, bipolar is like 200 per 100,000, schizophrenia is on the order of 500 per 100,000 in terms of completion.

Daniel: It’s in between those two. When I’m at a conference, I usually present early in the morning, so everyone’s carrying their Starbucks. I started to notice this early in my presenting career, and I would say, how many of you went to Starbucks? Knowing full well 70 percent of the audience has Starbucks in their hand. Now, imagine you woke up this morning, how many of you took a toll to get to this place? Because Florida has toll roads all over the place. Have Starbucks, took a toll. Now, imagine that you have to not do either of those things. How inconvenient would your morning have been? Now, you can’t do anything with your debit card today. How inconvenient would your day be? And you can’t talk to anyone about it, because you’ll have to admit your lies if you do. Now, how inconvenient would your day be?

I keep adding layers and layers until I get them to understand how cut off from just being themselves gambling will make them, because preserving the problem allows you to at least participate in the problem more. And so you will let yourself fall apart like that, just so you can have the chance to gamble again, when all these problems define every moment of your day.

Who’s at Risk?

Owen: So it’s devastating, common. Probably young men are more at risk than other populations, I’d guess, but I could be wrong.

Daniel: Females have their own appeal to gambling, too. Some gaming apps, like Candy Crush, mask a gambling process inside a video game to drive engagement and revenue. We call it gamblification of video games. People will not come to a therapist saying, I have a gambling problem, and they think it’s just Candy Crush, so they won’t even say, I have a Candy Crush problem, because what even is that? I’m talking to this MD or this PhD, I’m not gonna say I have a little problem with a video game on my phone.

But that’s what we want to hear, because then we can help them. The disconnect is there’s all these problems that don’t feel like the kind of problems you would go to therapy for. It just ruins your whole life before you realize I need to talk to someone about it.

Owen: The preconceived notion that it’s this group or that group is part of the problem.

Daniel: The average age that comes to mind of when’s the first time you placed a bet, and then in young adulthood you realize you have a gambling problem, it’s 12. It’s not 17, it’s not 18, it’s not 21, it’s 12.

This could be a scratch-off ticket that your grandparents put in your Christmas stocking or your birthday card. It could be, I got a deck of cards from my friend, and we used the little tabs on our soda cans as chips, and we learned how to play Texas Hold’em, because we saw it on ESPN and we thought it was cool. These are not things that are the worst thing in the world when you’re 12, but it creates a pathway in your brain that this is a fun thing to do, it’s social, it makes me feel smart and strategic.

That’s often for young boys, but girls could end up gambling in different ways, too. There are lottery tickets, there are slot machines, there are little apps on our phones that look like video games. Older adults, too. You could have the loss of your spouse or loved one. You have all this money, and you live at an assisted living very close to a casino, and they do a weekly trip because it’s low cost for them, it’s fun for most people, and you’re just expected to be responsible.

Training and Resources

Owen: What resources are available for clinicians who want to learn to treat this?

Daniel: If you want a niche in order to have a good business and learn a really powerful series of skills, you could do a training like the one that I built at the KindBridge Learning Center and get certified as a gambling counselor through the IGCCB, the International Problem Gambling and Gaming Certification Organization.

Owen: Is that available now?

Daniel: It absolutely is. We have a 30 CEU and 60 CEU training. It leads directly to being able to sit for the exam and become a certified gambling counselor. You can do case consultations with me, and we’ll work on when you start getting your gambling cases, just having that supervision and guidance to really understand the issue.

It’s really important with these clients that you are able to show them that you understand the games they are playing and the problems they are facing. Because if you try to copy and paste the exact philosophy of treating alcohol or cocaine or opiate use onto gambling, you’re going to miss things. There’s such a financial component, there’s such a deceit and relational devastation. Debt is hard to face, but when people are depressed, they don’t usually come into their therapy session trying to fix their debt. With gambling, you have the mental health side, and you have that crippling financial hole.

Technology and Process Addictions

Owen: My impression is that technology has made all of this worse, and faster.

Daniel: Sex and pornography usually has the greatest advancements of technology before we find a reasonable everyday use for it. VCRs, going back to that technology, really spread because of pornography footage getting copied to distribute it, and then eventually it ends up in living rooms and you can watch movies.

Owen: Hollywood and others rode on the coattails of pornography, because pornography built a distribution system that allowed media companies to distribute VHS tapes.

Daniel: And this goes back into ancient times, too. Whatever technology humans come up with, we figure out, can we have sex with it, and then can we use it for something worth our time?

Owen: There were some pretty hot tablets.

Daniel: Yeah, there were. This is not really a joke, that is absolutely true. So this is not a new problem, it’s just technology makes it move so much faster.

Thanks for reading!

—Owen

With gambling, you have the mental health side, and you have the crippling, often six-figure, maybe seven-figure financial hole that they’ve created for themselves.

Owen: And there are plenty of people who are willing to get you hooked on debt. Their entire industry is based on getting vulnerable people to take out more loans than they can practically afford.

Daniel: I’ve never tried to do this myself, because I don’t gamble, but from what I’ve heard from my clients, you can get more dollars approved for a personal loan in a casino than if you apply on Credit Karma or anywhere else. They want you to owe that money. Your wins did not even belong to you.

Owen: What’s the suicide rate, by the way? Because I focus a lot on this newsletter on suicide. How bad is that?

Daniel: It is comparable to disorders like bipolar disorder, and the only real psychiatric condition that has a higher suicide rate than gambling is schizophrenia.

Owen: So, bipolar is like 200 per 100,000, schizophrenia is on the order of 500 per 100,000 in terms of completion.

Daniel: It’s in between those two. When I’m at a conference, I usually present early in the morning, so everyone’s carrying their Starbucks. I started to notice this early in my presenting career, and I would say, how many of you went to Starbucks? Knowing full well 70 percent of the audience has Starbucks in their hand. Now, imagine you woke up this morning, how many of you took a toll to get to this place? Because Florida has toll roads all over the place. Have Starbucks, took a toll. Now, imagine that you have to not do either of those things. How inconvenient would your morning have been? Now, you can’t do anything with your debit card today. How inconvenient would your day be? And you can’t talk to anyone about it, because you’ll have to admit your lies if you do. Now, how inconvenient would your day be?

I keep adding layers and layers until I get them to understand how cut off from just being themselves gambling will make them, because preserving the problem allows you to at least participate in the problem more. And so you will let yourself fall apart like that, just so you can have the chance to gamble again, when all these problems define every moment of your day.

Who’s at Risk?

Owen: So it’s devastating, common. Probably young men are more at risk than other populations, I’d guess, but I could be wrong.

Daniel: Females have their own appeal to gambling, too. Some gaming apps, like Candy Crush, mask a gambling process inside a video game to drive engagement and revenue. We call it gamblification of video games. People will not come to a therapist saying, I have a gambling problem, and they think it’s just Candy Crush, so they won’t even say, I have a Candy Crush problem, because what even is that? I’m talking to this MD or this PhD, I’m not gonna say I have a little problem with a video game on my phone.

But that’s what we want to hear, because then we can help them. The disconnect is there’s all these problems that don’t feel like the kind of problems you would go to therapy for. It just ruins your whole life before you realize I need to talk to someone about it.

Owen: The preconceived notion that it’s this group or that group is part of the problem.

Daniel: The average age that comes to mind of when’s the first time you placed a bet, and then in young adulthood you realize you have a gambling problem, it’s 12. It’s not 17, it’s not 18, it’s not 21, it’s 12.

This could be a scratch-off ticket that your grandparents put in your Christmas stocking or your birthday card. It could be, I got a deck of cards from my friend, and we used the little tabs on our soda cans as chips, and we learned how to play Texas Hold’em, because we saw it on ESPN and we thought it was cool. These are not things that are the worst thing in the world when you’re 12, but it creates a pathway in your brain that this is a fun thing to do, it’s social, it makes me feel smart and strategic.

That’s often for young boys, but girls could end up gambling in different ways, too. There are lottery tickets, there are slot machines, there are little apps on our phones that look like video games. Older adults, too. You could have the loss of your spouse or loved one. You have all this money, and you live at an assisted living very close to a casino, and they do a weekly trip because it’s low cost for them, it’s fun for most people, and you’re just expected to be responsible.

Training and Resources

Owen: What resources are available for clinicians who want to learn to treat this?

Daniel: If you want a niche in order to have a good business and learn a really powerful series of skills, you could do a training like the one that I built at the KindBridge Learning Center and get certified as a gambling counselor through the IGCCB, the International Problem Gambling and Gaming Certification Organization.

Owen: Is that available now?

Daniel: It absolutely is. We have a 30 CEU and 60 CEU training. It leads directly to being able to sit for the exam and become a certified gambling counselor. You can do case consultations with me, and we’ll work on when you start getting your gambling cases, just having that supervision and guidance to really understand the issue.

It’s really important with these clients that you are able to show them that you understand the games they are playing and the problems they are facing. Because if you try to copy and paste the exact philosophy of treating alcohol or cocaine or opiate use onto gambling, you’re going to miss things. There’s such a financial component, there’s such a deceit and relational devastation. Debt is hard to face, but when people are depressed, they don’t usually come into their therapy session trying to fix their debt. With gambling, you have the mental health side, and you have that crippling financial hole.
